title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 433
paragraphs: When he was doing these things, Croesus the Lydian thought it right to admonish him with the following words: “O king, do not indulge your youthful heat and passion in everything, but restrain and hold yourself back. It is a good thing to be prudent, and forethought is wise. You, however, are putting to death men who are of your own people, condemning them on charges of no consequence, and putting men's sons to death as well. If you do many such things, beware that the Persians do not revolt from you. As for me, your father Cyrus gave me charge, earnestly bidding me admonish you and suggest whatever I might find to be good.” Thus he counseled him, showing goodwill toward him; but Cambyses answered: “Do you dare to counsel me — you who ruled your own country so excellently and advised my father so well when you urged him to cross the river Araxes and march against the Massagetai when they were willing to cross into our land, and so utterly ruined yourself through bad government of your own country, and utterly ruined Cyrus, who followed your counsel? However, you shall not escape punishment now, for know that I have long been seeking some pretext against you.” Having said this, he took up his bow intending to shoot him, but Croesus started up and ran out. So since he could not shoot him, he ordered his attendants to seize him and kill him. The attendants, however, knowing his moods, concealed Croesus, with the intention that if Cambyses should change his mind and want Croesus back, they might produce him and receive gifts as the reward for saving his life; but if he did not change his mind or feel any desire to have him back, then they might kill him. Not long afterwards Cambyses did in fact want Croesus back, and the attendants, noticing this, reported to him that he was still alive. Cambyses said he rejoiced with Croesus that he was still alive, but that those who had preserved him would not get off free — he would put them to death — and so he did.
